text: MGM Resorts International, a Delaware corporation incorporated in 1986, operates as a holding company and, through its subsidiaries, owns and manages integrated casino, hotel, and entertainment resorts in the United States and Macau. MGM Growth Properties LLC (“MGP”), a consolidated subsidiary of MGM Resorts, is structured as an umbrella partnership REIT (UPREIT), with substantially all of its assets owned by and its businesses conducted through MGM Growth Properties Operating Partnership LP (the “Operating Partnership”). Under a master lease agreement, a subsidiary of MGM Resorts (the “tenant”) leases real estate assets of The Mirage, Mandalay Bay, Luxor, New York-New York, Park MGM (branded as Monte Carlo prior to May 2018), Excalibur, The Park, Gold Strike Tunica, MGM Grand Detroit, Beau Rivage, Borgata, and MGM National Harbor from a subsidiary of the Operating Partnership (the “landlord”). The Company believes it owns or invests in some of the finest casino resorts globally and reinvests in its properties through renovations, new hotel rooms, restaurants, entertainment, and amenities to maintain competitive advantage. In August 2016, the Company acquired Boyd Gaming’s ownership interest in Borgata, which became a consolidated subsidiary, and subsequently MGP acquired Borgata’s real property. In December 2016, MGM National Harbor opened, and in October 2017, MGP acquired the long-term leasehold and real property associated with it. In February 2018, MGM Cotai opened on the Cotai Strip in Macau, and in August 2018, MGM Springfield opened in Springfield, Massachusetts. In July 2018, MGP acquired Northfield Park Associates, LLC (“Northfield”) for approximately $1.1 billion, and simultaneously entered into a management agreement with an affiliate of Hard Rock Café International (STP, Inc.). In September 2018, the Company agreed to acquire all operating assets of Northfield from MGP for approximately $275 million, subject to customary adjustments, with the transaction expected to close in the first half of 2019. In December 2018, the Company entered into a transaction with MGP for approximately $638 million in consideration for renovations to Park MGM and NoMad Las Vegas, with closing expected in the first quarter of 2019, subject to customary conditions. In January 2019, the Company completed the acquisition of Empire City Casino’s race track and casino for approximately $864 million, subject to adjustments, and MGP acquired the real property for approximately $634 million. In connection with this, the Company amended the existing master lease to lease back the real estate assets of Empire City and agreed to provide MGP a right of first offer on undeveloped land adjacent to the property for future gaming facility development. All casino resorts operate 24 hours a day except Empire City, which operates 20 hours a day. The Company’s domestic resorts include Bellagio, MGM Grand Las Vegas (including The Signature), Mandalay Bay (including Delano and Four Seasons), The Mirage, Luxor, New York-New York (including the Park), Excalibur, Park MGM (including NoMad Las Vegas), and Circus Circus Las Vegas on the Las Vegas Strip, and regional operations include MGM Grand Detroit, Beau Rivage, Gold Strike Tunica, Borgata, MGM National Harbor, and MGM Springfield. Over half of the net revenue from domestic resorts comes from non-gaming operations such as hotel, food and beverage, entertainment, and other amenities. The Company markets to diverse customer groups, including convention attendees, and relies on high customer volume to influence room and amenity pricing. Casino operations include slots, table games, and race and sports book wagering, with premium players accessing high-limit rooms and lounges. The Company owns approximately 56% of MGM China Holdings Limited, which owns and operates MGM Macau and MGM Cotai through MGM Grand Paradise, a Macau gaming subconcessionaire whose concession expires in 2020. Macau is the world’s largest gaming destination by revenue, and the Company expects growth in the Asian gaming market to increase visitation at its Macau properties. The Macau government prohibits new concessions or subconcessions but does not limit the number of casinos or gaming areas operated by existing concessionaires or subconcessionaires, though new casinos require government approval. The Company also has business activities through unconsolidated affiliates, including CityCenter Holdings, LLC, which it manages for a fee, and MGP’s Northfield. The company competes in highly competitive environments with gaming companies, hospitality firms, and non-gaming destinations like Hawaii, facing competition from state-sponsored lotteries, off-track wagering, card parlors, online gambling, and other legalized gaming. Primary competitive methods include locating in desirable markets, maintaining high-quality resorts with luxurious rooms, state-of-the-art convention facilities, and premier dining, entertainment, retail, and amenities; recruiting, training, and retaining qualified employees; offering unique entertainment; and developing distinctive marketing and customer loyalty programs. Customers include premium gaming, leisure and wholesale travel, business travelers, and group customers such as conventions and trade associations. Las Vegas Strip resorts compete with other hotel casinos on or near the Strip, in downtown Las Vegas (about five miles from the center), and elsewhere in the area, with new entrants expanding capacity or building new resorts. Growth in gaming outside Las Vegas increases competition in Las Vegas. Outside Nevada, resorts compete with other hotel casinos in their markets and surrounding regional gaming markets, where location is critical, and also face competition from gaming operations in neighboring jurisdictions and other leisure destinations. In Macau, the three primary customer bases are VIP casino gaming, main floor gaming, and slot machine operations. VIP gaming is sourced externally through gaming promoters who offer credit and complimentary services and are compensated via revenue-sharing and turnover-based commissions; in-house VIP players receive commissions based on rolling chip turnover. Main floor players do not receive commissions, and the profit contribution from this segment exceeds that of VIP due to commission costs. Gaming revenues from main floors have grown significantly and represent the most potential for sustainable growth. To target premium main floor players, premium gaming lounges and stadium-style electronic table games terminals (including table games and slots) have been introduced. VIP gaming uses special purpose nonnegotiable gaming chips to track wagering, with promoter commissions based on a percentage of gross table games win or turnover and a complimentary allowance based on turnover, recorded as a reduction of casino revenue. In-house VIP commissions are based on rolling chip turnover and are also recorded as a reduction of casino revenue. Key competitors in Macau include five other gaming concessionaires and subconcessionaires; additional concessions could increase competition. Competition also comes from major gaming centers in Asia and globally, including Singapore, Korea, Australia, New Zealand, Malaysia, Vietnam, Cambodia, the Philippines, Russia, cruise ships in Asia, and unlicensed gaming operations. Marketing efforts include advertising on radio, television, internet, billboards, newspapers, magazines, direct mail, email, and social media, as well as through regional offices. Direct marketing uses advanced analytics to identify customer preferences and predict behavior. M life Rewards is a tiered loyalty program that offers benefits across resorts in gaming and non-gaming areas, encouraging total spend within the company’s resorts. The Golden Lion Club is offered for gaming-focused customers at MGM China. Loyalty programs are structured by member value and tier level to allow progressive access to services. The company’s strategy includes operational enhancements, financial strength, corporate social responsibility, geographic expansion, and business model innovation. The company is recognized globally for awards, including Four and Five Diamond designations from the American Automobile Association and multiple Four and Five Star designations from Forbes Travel Guide, as well as certifications in Corporate Social Responsibility. Technology is used to maximize revenue, drive operational efficiency, and serve customers effectively, with information technology automating operations, using data and analytics for decision-making, and applying a cloud-first strategy. The eCommerce platform enables guests and business partners to create all-inclusive experiences with real-time recommendations based on preferences. Employees and management are central to success, with heavy investment in recruiting, training, motivation, and retention, supported by programs such as MGM Resorts University and leadership training. Corporate Social Responsibility is linked to long-term sustainability and profitability, guided by core values of integrity, inclusion, teamwork, and excellence. Four strategic pillars include fostering diversity and inclusion, investing in community, caring for one another, and environmental sustainability. The company promotes diversity to attract talent, drive innovation, expand markets, and strengthen community ties. It creates economic opportunity for local residents, supports education and workforce development, engages local businesses, and promotes responsible gaming through tools like GameSense. Employee-driven initiatives include the MGM Resorts Foundation, Employee Volunteer Program, and Corporate Giving Program, with U.S. employees investing over 123,000 hours of volunteer service in 2018 and a 71% participation rate in giving. Environmental sustainability efforts include energy and water conservation, recycling, waste management, sustainable supply chains, and green construction. Several resorts, including Aria, Vdara, Bellagio, Delano, Mandalay Bay, MGM Grand Detroit, and CityCenter (Aria, Vdara, Veer), have earned Green Key certifications, with Aria, Vdara, Bellagio, Delano, Mandalay Bay, and MGM Grand Detroit receiving the highest “Five Green Key” rating. CityCenter is one of the world’s largest private sustainable developments with six LEED® Gold certifications from the U.S. Green Building Council, and MGM National Harbor, The Park, and T-Mobile Arena have also received LEED® Gold certification. At MGM China, efforts in energy efficiency, indoor air quality, and environmental stewardship have led to inclusion in the Hang Seng Corporate Sustainability Benchmark Index and the China Green Building (Macau) Design label for MGM Cotai. It leverages management expertise and well-recognized brands through strategic partnerships and international expansion. The gaming industry is highly regulated, and the company must maintain licenses and pay gaming taxes to operate. Each casino is subject to extensive regulation under the laws of its jurisdiction, which generally address the responsibility, financial stability, and character of owners, managers, and those with financial interests. Violations in one jurisdiction could lead to disciplinary action in others. Additional regulations cover alcoholic beverages, smoking, employees, currency transactions, taxation, zoning, building codes (including the Americans with Disabilities Act), construction, land use, and marketing, and the company is subject to anti-money laundering and reporting requirements. The company faces significant risks related to its substantial indebtedness, including approximately $15.3 billion of principal debt outstanding as of December 31, 2018, which included $750 million in borrowings, $1.5 billion in available borrowing capacity under its senior secured credit facility, $2.4 billion and $2.8 billion of debt under the MGM China and Operating Partnership credit facilities, respectively, and $1.9 billion of senior notes outstanding from the Operating Partnership. An increase in interest rates would raise the cost of debt and reduce available cash flow. The company does not guarantee MGM China’s or the Operating Partnership’s debt obligations, and if those entities fail to generate sufficient cash flow, the company’s ability to invest in them is limited by covenants in its senior secured credit facility. The substantial debt and financial commitments could negatively impact operations, limit flexibility in responding to business changes, restrict access to additional funding for working capital, capital expenditures, debt service, or strategic initiatives, make debt payments more difficult, and place the company at a competitive disadvantage compared to less-leveraged firms. The company’s businesses are capital-intensive, requiring ongoing capital investment to maintain, modernize, and refurbish owned, leased, and managed resorts, with a requirement under the master lease to spend at least 1% of actual adjusted net revenues on capital expenditures. Development projects, such as potential future integrated resorts in Japan, and acquisitions could require significant capital, additional debt, third-party guarantees, or contingent liabilities, all of which could harm the company’s business and financial results. Current and future economic, capital, and credit market conditions could impair the company’s ability to service or refinance debt and fund planned expenditures, depending on future cash flow, distributions from unconsolidated affiliates like CityCenter, MGM China, and the Operating Partnership, access to borrowing under the senior secured credit facility, or the ability to secure new debt. The company has significant debt maturing in 2020 and beyond, and its ability to refinance will depend on economic and credit market conditions. Failure to refinance could force the company to seek alternative financing, dispose of assets, or reduce capital expenditures, with no assurance such alternatives would be available on acceptable terms or without breaching existing debt agreements. The senior secured credit facility and other senior debt agreements contain restrictions that limit the company’s ability to pay dividends, repurchase equity, prepay debt, incur additional debt, create liens, sell assets, consolidate, enter into affiliate transactions, or engage in sale and lease-back arrangements. Breach of these covenants could result in default and acceleration of debt obligations, triggering cross-defaults under other long-term debt agreements. The facility also requires compliance with financial covenants, including maximum total net leverage ratio, maximum first lien net leverage ratio, and minimum interest coverage ratio. MGM Grand Paradise and MGM China are co-borrowers under an amended and restated credit facility, and the Operating Partnership is a borrower under its senior secured credit facility, both of which impose financial covenants and operating restrictions on them and their subsidiaries, including limitations on paying dividends, incurring debt, making investments, merging, or transferring assets. The company is required to pay a significant portion of its cash flow as fixed and percentage rent under the master lease. For the third lease year beginning April 1, 2018, annual rent payments were $770 million, with fixed annual escalators of 2% in the second through sixth years and potential additional 2% increases thereafter based on an adjusted net revenue to rent ratio, and possible percentage rent increases in year six and every five years thereafter based on average annual net revenue over the prior five years. These obligations may make it harder to meet debt obligations, increase vulnerability to economic downturns, reduce cash flow available for working capital, capital expenditures, development, and other corporate purposes, limit flexibility in responding to business changes, restrict major transactions, and result in loss of rights to all leased properties if rent or other obligations are not met, as the master lease is a single unitary lease with cross-collateralization. The company competes against major resorts with established brands, smaller hotel offerings, and peer-to-peer rental platforms, and faces increased competition from new distribution channels, consumer technology innovations, and industry transformations. Most jurisdictions impose numerical or geographical limits on new gaming licenses, and new gaming operations may be restricted to specific locations, leading to intense competition for new opportunities, including acquisitions. Some jurisdictions, such as Nevada and New Jersey, have legalized online gaming, and Illinois has legalized video gaming terminals. The business is affected by economic and market conditions in operating jurisdictions and customer locations, particularly sensitive to reductions in discretionary consumer and corporate spending on hotels, casino resorts, trade shows, and business development. Economic contraction, uncertainty, or perceptions of weak economic conditions may reduce demand for luxury amenities. Changes in consumer spending or preferences, driven by factors such as rising travel costs, unstable job markets, disposable income or wealth, disease outbreaks, or fears of war or terrorism, can influence demand. Consumer preferences evolve due to demographic changes, such as increased demand for non-gaming offerings. Success depends on anticipating and responding to these trends; failure to do so may harm results of operations. Aria, Bellagio, and MGM Grand Las Vegas are particularly affected by economic conditions in the Far East, while all Nevada resorts are affected by U.S. and especially California economic conditions. A recession or slowdown is likely to reduce visitation and harm operating results, as seen during prior downturns. Since a significant number of customers to MGM Macau and MGM Cotai come from mainland China, economic conditions in China impact financial prospects. A slowdown in China’s growth or changes in travel and currency conversion restrictions—such as those from China’s anti-corruption campaign, tighter liquidity from non-bank lending, and increased ATM limits on pataca withdrawals—could reduce visitor numbers or spending. In July 2017, the Chinese government and Macau authorities implemented facial recognition on ATM machines to enforce “know your customer” rules for mainland Chinese cardholders, and in November 2017, new rules were introduced to control cross-border cash and bearer instrument transport. It is unclear whether these measures will continue, become more restrictive, or be re-imposed. These developments have reduced or may further reduce mainland Chinese visitors to Macau, negatively impacting tourism and the gaming industry. Future policies that freeze or cancel labor imports could increase labor costs. Additionally, with new casino projects opening and under construction, existing transportation infrastructure may need expansion to handle increased visitation. Property and equipment are stated at cost, with assets acquired through business combinations recognized at fair value. Maintenance and repairs that do not materially add to value or prolong asset life are expensed as incurred. Depreciation and amortization are on a straight-line basis over estimated useful lives. Direct costs of construction, including architect and contractor fees, property taxes, and design and construction subsidiary costs, are capitalized. Interest costs on major development projects are capitalized using the weighted-average cost of outstanding borrowings, beginning when construction starts and ceasing when construction is substantially complete or development is suspended for more than a brief period. Judgments are required to determine whether expenditures are maintenance or capital, whether existing assets are being replaced or impaired, and the estimated useful lives of assets, which are based on experience, engineering studies, and usage estimates. When events or circumstances change the estimated useful life of an asset, the change is accounted for prospectively. The company evaluates property and equipment and other long-lived assets for impairment based on whether they are classified as held for sale or to be held and used. For assets classified as held for sale, the asset is recognized at the lower of carrying value or fair market value less costs of disposal, estimated based on comparable sales, offers received, or discounted cash flow models. For assets to be held and used, impairment is reviewed when indicators exist, and the undiscounted future cash flows are compared to carrying value. If undiscounted cash flows exceed carrying value, no impairment is indicated; if not, an impairment is recorded based on fair value, typically measured using a discounted cash flow model with a weighted-average cost of capital derived from a standard capital asset pricing model based on guideline companies in the industry. For assets under development, future cash flows include remaining construction costs. All recognized impairment losses are recorded prospectively.
